news.title: Scammers Are Posing as Computer 'Rescue' Companies — Don't Pay Them a Dime
news.excerpt: Crooks are now posing as computer "rescue" companies to steal money. Researchers say a group calling itself Ransom Busters has been emailing people right after their computers are attacked — sometimes before the attack is even public — and offering to "recover" their files for a fee. Researchers believe the "rescuers" are the same crooks behind the attacks. If you get an email or call like this, don't pay, don't reply, and don't call the number in the message. Real help never comes from a stranger demanding money.

news.title: Hackers Are Breaking Into Windows Computers Right Now — Update Today
news.excerpt: The federal government's cyber-watchdog agency warned Wednesday that hackers are actively breaking into Windows computers through a weakness Microsoft already fixed back in April. If your computer hasn't installed the update, a crook can get in over the internet — no clicking, no tricking you — and take it over. The fix takes two minutes: press the Start button, type "check for updates," open it, install whatever it finds, then turn your computer off and back on.

news.title: Fake 'Download' Pages Can Take Over Your Browser — Never Copy-Paste From a Website
news.excerpt: A new bad program called AmnesiaStealer is spreading through fake "download" pages. The page tells you to copy a command and paste it — and once it's in, it takes over the program you use to go on the internet and can steal your saved passwords. Real download pages never ask you to copy and paste commands. If one does, close the tab. Only download programs from the maker's real website, and keep your computer's free updates turned on.

news.title: Crooks Are Buying Expired Websites — a Site You Save Could Become a Trap
news.excerpt: Crooks are buying up expired website addresses — spending millions to do it — and turning them into traps that install bad programs or run scams. Every day, thousands of website addresses lapse, and security researchers say criminals snap them up to fool people who've trusted those sites for years. If a familiar website suddenly looks different, begs you to install something, or flashes alarming pop-ups, close it. Type the company's address yourself instead, and never click a link that pushes you to a site.

news.title: Fake Job Offer Emails Are Installing Bad Programs — Don't Open the Attachment
news.excerpt: Scammers are sending fake job offer emails — notes about a "position" you never applied for, with a file attached. Opening that file quietly installs a bad program on your computer, and security researchers say this newest wave is already spreading. If a job offer shows up out of nowhere, don't open the attachment. Delete the message. Looking for work? Go straight to the company's website and apply there. Never click a link in an email that's trying to hand you a job you didn't ask for.

posts.title: Hackers found a way into Macs over the internet and are using them to mine digital money — update macOS today
posts.summary: Open System Settings, click General, then Software Update, and install whatever Apple offers — it's free and takes about 10 minutes. If you can't update right away, you can also turn off Screen Sharing (System Settings → General → Sharing → Screen Sharing) unless you actually use it.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize their Mac has a feature called Screen Sharing that lets another computer take over the screen — and on many machines it's left on without anyone knowing. The honest answer is that this isn't a Mac problem to panic about, it's an update problem: install the fix and the hole is closed.

posts.title: Firefox just shipped its August 18 security update — check yours free at firefox.com in 2 minutes
posts.summary: Open Firefox, click the three-line menu in the top corner, choose Help then About Firefox, and let it finish updating — it's free and takes about 2 minutes. If it says "Firefox is up to date," you're good. If you don't have Firefox at all, download it free from firefox.com.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize their browser updates itself quietly — until an update gets stuck and they keep browsing on an old, unprotected copy. The honest answer is that the 2 minutes it takes to check Firefox is some of the cheapest insurance you'll ever buy, and I say that to everyone who walks in this door.

posts.title: Internet down? Check the free Xfinity Outage Map before you blame your equipment — xfinity.com/support/statusmap
posts.summary: When your internet drops, first check whether the whole neighborhood is down. Open the Xfinity Outage Map at xfinity.com/support/statusmap, type in your service address, and it shows you if there's an outage and when it's expected back. If the map shows nothing, the trouble is inside your house — that's when you call the shop.
posts.truth: I see this all the time: a customer buys brand-new equipment because the internet went out, and it turns out the whole street was down and the cable company fixed it before they even got home. The honest answer is check the map first — it can save you a hundred dollars and a trip to the store.

posts.title: Your info leaked? Freeze your credit free at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion
posts.summary: A credit freeze stops crooks from opening credit cards or loans in your name — and it's free by federal law. Do it online at equifax.com, experian.com, and transunion.com; it takes about 20 minutes total, and you can freeze a child's credit too.
posts.tip: A credit freeze stops crooks from opening credit cards or loans in your name — and it's free by federal law. Do it online at equifax.com, experian.com, and transunion.com; it takes about 20 minutes total, and you can freeze a child's credit too.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that after a leak, crooks don't come after your money — they come after your name. A freeze is the one thing that stops them before they open anything.

posts.title: Type with your voice for free — Windows Voice Typing is built into Windows 11, press the Windows key + H
posts.summary: Click into any text box, press the Windows key + H, and start talking — Windows Voice Typing types your words for you, free, with nothing to download. It's already on your Windows 11 computer; if nothing happens, check that the microphone is turned on at Settings > Privacy & security > Microphone.
posts.truth: I see this all the time: somebody's hands hurt, or they never got comfortable typing, so they just don't write emails or long messages at all. Most people don't realize their computer already has a free speech-to-text helper sitting right inside it. The honest answer is you don't need to buy a thing — Windows Voice Typing is already there, and once folks try it, half of them never go back to pecking at the keys. It's not a gimmick; it's how a lot of people get their words out without pain.

posts.title: Your PC feels slow? Task Manager shows what's eating it — built into Windows, press Ctrl+Shift+Esc
posts.summary: Press Ctrl+Shift+Esc to open Task Manager — it's built into Windows and shows every program running on your computer. Look at the top of the list: whatever is using the most working memory is usually the troublemaker. To close a stuck program, click it, then click End Task.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that "slow computer" almost always has a name — a program quietly running in the background. I see this all the time: it's not that the computer is old, it's that something is hogging it.

posts.title: Your computer has a check-engine light hidden inside — read it free with CrystalDiskInfo before it quits on you
posts.summary: Download CrystalDiskInfo free from crystalmark.info and open it. The big box at the top shows your computer's storage health — think of it as the check-engine light for the part that holds all your files. If it says "Good," you're fine. If it says "Caution" or "Bad," don't wait — bring the computer in and we'll save what we can while there's still time.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that the part that holds your files usually gives weeks of warning before it dies — it just doesn't know how to tell you. I see this all the time: the warning was sitting there on the screen, nobody looked, and by the time the computer quit, the family pictures were gone for good.

posts.title: Can't open that file your bank or lawyer sent? 7-Zip opens it free — download at 7-zip.org
posts.summary: Files that end in .zip or .rar are just folders squeezed into one file — and Windows won't open all of them. Download 7-Zip free from 7-zip.org, install it (takes about a minute), then right-click the file and choose "7-Zip > Extract here" to get your documents out.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that when a file won't open, it's usually not broken — it's just bundled up. I've had customers delete an important file thinking it was corrupt when it was one right-click away from opening.

posts.title: Email says 'file too big'? WeTransfer sends it free — no account needed at wetransfer.com
posts.summary: Go to wetransfer.com, add your file (up to 3 GB free), type the person's email address, and hit send — they get a link to download it. No account, no software, works in any browser.
posts.truth: The honest answer is email was never built to carry photos and video. When a customer tells me their pictures won't send, I tell them to stop fighting the email and send a link instead.

posts.title: Microsoft's August Windows update closes 400+ security holes — get it tonight at Settings > Windows Update
posts.summary: Microsoft shipped its August 2026 Windows update on Tuesday and says to install it within days — it closes more than 400 security holes in Windows. Open Settings > Windows Update, click Check for updates, let it finish, and restart your computer once. Free, and it takes about ten minutes.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize their computer only stays safe if the updates actually get installed. I see machines come in where the last update went through months ago because somebody clicked "remind me later" one too many times. The honest answer is a ten-minute update tonight is a whole lot cheaper than a long afternoon at the shop after something bad happens. Microsoft built the update to do the work for you — you just have to let it run.
